prompt: What is the C−C−C bond angle in cyclopropane, in degrees?
explanation: The three carbons of cyclopropane form a triangle, so the C−C−C bond angles are 60°, far from the normal 109° tetrahedral value. This is the main source of cyclopropane's strain.

prompt: What is the primary reason cyclopropane is the most strained of all rings?

choices.text: Angle strain from its 60° C−C−C bond angles
Torsional strain from eclipsed C−H bonds
choices.why: Cyclopropane does have considerable torsional strain, but the section names angle strain as the primary cause.

choices.text: Steric strain between large groups crowded together
choices.why: Cyclopropane carries only hydrogens on its ring carbons; its strain comes from bond angles and eclipsing, not crowded groups.

choices.text: Its C−C bonds are unusually short
choices.why: The section attributes the strain to distorted bond angles, not to bond length.

explanation: Cyclopropane is the most strained of all rings, primarily due to the angle strain caused by its 60° C−C−C bond angles. Torsional strain from eclipsed neighboring C−H bonds adds to it (Figure 4.4.1).

prompt: Why does cyclopropane have considerable torsional strain?

choices.text: The C−H bonds on neighboring carbon atoms are eclipsed
Its C−C−C bond angles are 60° instead of 109°
choices.why: That is the cause of its angle strain. Torsional strain comes from eclipsed bonds on neighboring carbons.

choices.text: Its ring hydrogens are staggered
choices.why: Staggered bonds have no torsional strain. In planar cyclopropane, neighboring C−H bonds cannot avoid being eclipsed.

choices.text: Its bonds are bent
choices.why: Bent bonds are how the orbitals cope with the small angle; they explain the weak C−C bonds, not the torsional strain.

explanation: In addition to angle strain, cyclopropane has considerable torsional strain because the C−H bonds on neighboring carbon atoms are eclipsed, as the Newman projection in Figure 4.4.1 shows.

prompt: How does the hybrid-orbital model account for cyclopropane's 60° bond angles?

choices.text: The orbitals can't point directly toward each other, so they overlap at a slight angle, forming bent bonds
The carbons rehybridize so that their orbitals point 60° apart
choices.why: The section does not invoke a change in hybridization; it explains the angle by orbitals overlapping off the line between the nuclei.

choices.text: The orbitals point directly at each other, just as in an unstrained alkane
choices.why: Head-on overlap is what gives maximum bonding in an unstrained alkane. In cyclopropane the geometry prevents it.

choices.text: The C−C bonds are π bonds rather than σ bonds
choices.why: Cyclopropane is a saturated alkane; its bonds are σ bonds whose orbitals overlap at an angle.

explanation: In an unstrained alkane, maximum bonding is achieved when the overlapping orbitals point directly toward each other. In cyclopropane they can't; instead, they overlap at a slight angle, so cyclopropane has bent bonds.

prompt: What is the strength of a C−C bond in cyclopropane, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Because of its bent bonds, a C−C bond in cyclopropane is only 255 kJ/mol (61 kcal/mol), compared with 370 kJ/mol (88 kcal/mol) for a C−C bond in open-chain propane.

prompt: Compared with typical alkane C−C bonds, how do cyclopropane's bent C−C bonds behave?

choices.text: They are weaker and more reactive
They are stronger and less reactive
choices.why: Bent bonds overlap less effectively than head-on bonds, so they are weaker: 255 kJ/mol versus 370 kJ/mol in propane.

choices.text: They are weaker but less reactive
choices.why: Weaker bonds are easier to break; the section describes them as weaker and more reactive.

choices.text: They are the same as in any other alkane
choices.why: Cyclopropane's orbitals can't point directly toward each other, which changes both strength and reactivity.

explanation: Because the orbitals overlap at a slight angle, cyclopropane bonds are weaker and more reactive than typical alkane bonds: 255 kJ/mol for a C−C bond in cyclopropane versus 370 kJ/mol in open-chain propane.

prompt: What is the total strain energy of cyclopropane, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Cyclopropane's total strain is 115 kJ/mol (27.5 kcal/mol), the largest of any ring, nearly matched by cyclobutane at 110 kJ/mol.

prompt: What is the total strain energy of cyclobutane, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Cyclobutane's total strain is 110 kJ/mol (26.4 kcal/mol), nearly the same as cyclopropane's 115 kJ/mol: it has less angle strain but more torsional strain.

prompt: Why is the total strain of cyclobutane nearly the same as that of cyclopropane?

choices.text: Cyclobutane has less angle strain but more torsional strain, because it has more ring hydrogens
Cyclobutane has the same bond angles as cyclopropane
choices.why: A four-membered ring has larger bond angles than a three-membered ring, so cyclobutane has less angle strain.

choices.text: Cyclobutane has more angle strain but less torsional strain
choices.why: It is the other way around: cyclobutane's angles are closer to tetrahedral, but its extra ring hydrogens add torsional strain.

choices.text: Both rings are completely flat with all C−H bonds eclipsed
choices.why: Cyclobutane is not quite flat; one carbon lies about 25° above the plane of the other three, which reduces eclipsing.

explanation: Cyclobutane has less angle strain than cyclopropane but more torsional strain because of its larger number of ring hydrogens. The two effects nearly cancel: 110 kJ/mol for cyclobutane versus 115 kJ/mol for cyclopropane.

prompt: In the conformation of cyclobutane, about how many degrees does one carbon atom lie above the plane of the other three?
explanation: Cyclobutane is not quite flat but is slightly bent so that one carbon atom lies about 25° above the plane of the other three (Figure 4.4.2).

prompt: What is the effect of cyclobutane's slight bend out of planarity?

choices.text: It increases angle strain but decreases torsional strain, reaching a minimum-energy balance
It decreases both angle strain and torsional strain
choices.why: Bending squeezes the bond angles further from tetrahedral, so angle strain goes up; only torsional strain goes down.

choices.text: It decreases angle strain but increases torsional strain
choices.why: That reverses the trade-off. Bending moves neighboring C−H bonds away from eclipsing, lowering torsional strain at the cost of angle strain.

choices.text: It removes all eclipsing, making cyclobutane strain-free
choices.why: Neighboring C−H bonds are only "not quite eclipsed" (Figure 4.4.2), and the total strain is still 110 kJ/mol.

explanation: The effect of the slight bend is to increase angle strain but to decrease torsional strain, until a minimum-energy balance between the two opposing effects is achieved. The Newman projection in Figure 4.4.2 shows neighboring C−H bonds are not quite eclipsed.

prompt: What is the total strain energy of cyclopentane, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Baeyer predicted cyclopentane to be nearly strain-free, but it actually has a total strain energy of 26 kJ/mol (6.2 kcal/mol).

prompt: What strain would cyclopentane have if it were planar?

choices.text: Practically no angle strain, but a large torsional strain
Large angle strain, but no torsional strain
choices.why: A planar five-membered ring has angles close to tetrahedral. Its problem is that every pair of neighboring C−H bonds would be eclipsed.

choices.text: No strain at all, as Baeyer predicted
choices.why: Baeyer considered only angle strain. Cyclopentane actually has 26 kJ/mol of strain, and a planar ring would have large torsional strain.

choices.text: Mostly steric strain between crowded hydrogens
choices.why: The section names torsional strain from eclipsing as the problem with planar cyclopentane.

explanation: Although planar cyclopentane has practically no angle strain, it has a large torsional strain. That is why cyclopentane twists into a puckered, nonplanar conformation.

prompt: Which describes the actual conformation of cyclopentane?

choices.text: Puckered: four carbons are in approximately the same plane, with the fifth bent out of the plane
Completely planar, with all five carbons in one plane
choices.why: A planar ring would have large torsional strain, so cyclopentane twists out of planarity.

choices.text: Puckered: three carbons in a plane, with the other two bent above it
choices.why: In cyclopentane, carbons 1, 2, 3, and 4 are nearly coplanar and only carbon 5 is out of the plane (Figure 4.4.3).

choices.text: Puckered so that all neighboring C−H bonds are exactly eclipsed
choices.why: Puckering does the opposite: most of the hydrogens end up nearly staggered with respect to their neighbors.

explanation: Cyclopentane adopts a puckered, nonplanar conformation that balances increased angle strain against decreased torsional strain. Four of the carbons are in approximately the same plane, the fifth is bent out of it, and most hydrogens are nearly staggered (Figure 4.4.3).

prompt: Which list puts cyclopropane, cyclobutane, and cyclopentane in order of decreasing total strain?

choices.text: Cyclopropane > cyclobutane > cyclopentane
Cyclobutane > cyclopropane > cyclopentane
choices.why: Cyclobutane's extra torsional strain brings it close to cyclopropane, but not past it: 110 kJ/mol versus 115 kJ/mol.

choices.text: Cyclopentane > cyclobutane > cyclopropane
choices.why: That is the order of increasing strain. Cyclopropane is the most strained of all rings.

choices.text: Cyclopropane > cyclopentane > cyclobutane
choices.why: Cyclopentane's strain (26 kJ/mol) is far below cyclobutane's (110 kJ/mol).

explanation: The total strain energies given in the section are 115 kJ/mol for cyclopropane, 110 kJ/mol for cyclobutane, and 26 kJ/mol for cyclopentane.
